correctness.rationale: For the integral companion matrix M, direct multiplication gives \(M^7=I+2C\) and \(M^{14}=I+4B\). Integral inverse powers yield \(w_{-4}=(-1,0,1)\), with first coordinates of \(Cw_{-4}\) and \(Bw_{-4}\) equal to 1 and 5. The binomial bound \(\nu_2(4^j\binom{m}{j})\geq\nu_2(m)+3\) for \(j\geq2\) proves the exact valuations on indices \(n=7s-4\). A complete 14-class mod-4 check and the mod-8 increment \(e_1Bw_5=148\) settle all remaining classes. The valuation classes are explicit arithmetic progressions, giving densities and the exact finite period errors \([-5/7,4/7]\), \([-3/7,9/7]\), and \([-15/28,6/7]\). Higher classes are single progressions with error \(<1\). Equality at \(C_1(4)-12/7=9/7\) proves sharpness. A separately implemented modular recurrence tests 100001 terms and separate matrix exponentiation and rational periodic counts agree. Finite computations support but do not replace the infinite argument.

value.rationale: The motivating paper explicitly treats Narayana values one away from 1 at prime three, and the binary analogue supplies a natural complementary exact invariant. The matrix proof isolates a genuine negative-index integer root that governs an infinite tower of valuations. The result determines every value, its exact rational natural frequency, and an optimal discrepancy 9/7 uniformly over both counting cutoff and valuation level. This is a natural complete classification with quantitative arithmetic content, not a routine example or arbitrary finite range.
